newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia deports 10 Timor meeting activists.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia deports 10 Timor meeting activists.

text.p: Malaysia on Monday deported the 10 remaining foreign human rights activists who took part in a short-lived conference on East Timor at the weekend and freed a foreign journalist who covered the event.
The conference, held ahead of Tuesday's anniversary of the 1991 killing by Indonesian troops of at least 50 demonstrators in East Timor's capital of Dili, was broken up by protesters.
An Immigration Department spokesperson at Kuala Lumpur's international airport said the 10, all Filipinos, left shortly after 10 a.m. (0200 GMT) for Manila.
They chanted "viva East Timor, viva East Timor" before entering the departure hall.
"This assured us how we should fight further. We should unite and I think we are more united now," Augusto Miclat, one of the deportees, told Reuters.
Thirty-six foreign activists were expelled on Sunday.
They included two Roman Catholic bishops -- Aloisuis Nobuo Somo of Nagoya, Japan and Hilton Deakin of Melbourne, Australia.
Police also released Asiaweek's correspondent in Kuala Lumpur, Roger Mitton, on Monday.

He was detained along with the foreign activists, another foreign journalist and dozens of local activists after a youth group allied to the government stormed Saturday's meeting, shouting slogans and singing patriotic songs.
The conference had been condemned by the government as damaging to its relations with Indonesia.
"It's not very pleasant in there," Mitton, a British national, told reporters outside the police station, before he was advised by his lawyer to say nothing more.
On Sunday, police freed the Singapore-based correspondent of the Australia Broadcasting Corporation, Catherine McGrath, and 26 local activists.
Her husband, Nicholas Stuart, told Reuters in Singapore that she expected to appear in a Malaysian court on unspecified charges later this month.
Thirty activists were still being detained. Organisers of the conference said they hoped they will be released on Monday.

Debbie Stothard, a spokesperson for the organisers, told reporters they have been instructed by the police to stop making statements. "Otherwise, they said they will slow down the process of releasing the rest," she said.
Sanusi Osman, a member of the conference organising committee, said those still in detention were maintaining a hunger strike until their release.

Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the government did not sanction the actions of the group which broke up the conference, although the youths belonged to groups allied to the three main political parties in the ruling coalition of Prime Minister Mohamad Mahathir.
"They acted on their own. I was not notifed by them," he told reporters on Sunday.
Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, leader of the Mahathir's United Malays National Organisation's youth wing, said on Sunday he ordered the youth group to take action to stop the conference.
Two of the deportees, Australian Andrew McNaughtan, 42, and Japanese Ihiro Kimura, 21, said Saturday's meeting in a Kuala Lumpur hotel had just begun when the youth group members stormed in.
"They ran amok, overturning chairs...and screaming...They were extremely threatening," McNaughtan told Reuters on Sunday after arriving in Manila.
